findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: Adult Social Care Older People services overspent by £8.9m; residential care unit costs and community support usage above budget.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care & Health directorate shows a net overspend of £9.1m. The primary driver is Older People Residential Care Services at +£6.4m, caused by average placement costs being higher than budget and lower-than-expected income from service user contributions (reflecting lower numbers paying full cost of care). A secondary pressure is Older People Community Based Services at +£2.1m, driven by higher Direct Payments volumes and lower income from client charges. These service lines sit within a long-term support division budgeted at £696.6m.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a large cost base (£786.7m budget, 47% of General Fund) with inelastic demand. Rising unit costs and usage pressures here indicate demographic and social care market pressures that are structural and likely to recur.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care & Health total budget £786.7m, forecast £795.8m (overspend £9.1m or 1.2%). Older People residential care overspend £6.4m, community services overspend £2.1m.
findings.quote: Pressures on this service line relate to the average costs of placements being higher than budgeted for which has been impacted by undeliverable savings, alongside reduced levels of income which is due to a combination of factors including reductions in the number of service users who pay for the full cost of their care.

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: Adult Social Care and Children's Services forecast to deliver 86-90% of savings targets; strategic service changes slipping.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care forecast to deliver £37.3m of £41.7m savings (89.6%), with £2.0m shortfall due to delayed implementation of a new Older People Residential & Nursing contract planned for Q2/3 rather than Q1. Children, Young People & Education forecast to deliver £18.4m of £21.3m (86.4%), with £0.953m of an invest-to-save in-house residential scheme not landing due to delayed home openings, £0.704m of residential special schools savings unachieved, and £0.601m of legal services efficiencies depending on Court proceedings acceleration.
findings.matters: Large service directorates are not delivering planned savings at the expected pace. Commissioning and strategic transformation milestones (contract mobilizations, new service models, facility openings) are slipping, indicating either over-ambitious targets or constrained delivery capability.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care: £41.7m target, £37.3m forecast (89.6%), £2.0m shortfall. Children, Young People & Education: £21.3m target, £18.4m forecast (86.4%), principal shortfalls £0.953m residential units, £0.704m schools, £0.601m legal.
findings.quote: A new Older People Residential & Nursing (OPRN) contract is planned for Quarter 2/3 which will introduce a new sustainable pricing model. Ahead of implementation ASC are managing cost pressures during the transition period ensuring affordability of all new placements until the new contract is mobilised.

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: Early debt redemption of £60m in 2025-26 generated £0.683m discount and £2.420m annual interest saving.
findings.detail: The council repaid £50m of debt in September 2025 and £10m in March 2025 ahead of maturity, obtaining a 10-year discount of £0.683m and achieving an annual interest cost saving of £2.420m. This was deliberate treasury strategy to lock in savings at favourable relative rates. However, the report notes that this action reduced cash balances and created short-term borrowing requirements, indicating tight liquidity management.
findings.matters: Early redemption reflects active debt management and sound rate-risk positioning. However, it reduced liquidity headroom and necessitated compensating short-term borrowing, indicating the council is managing cash flow tightly without significant buffer.
findings.figures: Debt redemptions £50m (September 2025) and £10m (March 2025), discount £0.683m, annual interest saving £2.420m.
findings.quote: Annual discount received for 10 years on £50m early debt redemption in September 2025 and £10m in March 2025 ... Impact on debt interest costs of £50m early debt redemption in 2025-26

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: General Fund reserves drawn down by £21.4m to fund in-year overspend; will fall to minimum threshold of 5.1%.
findings.detail: The £21.4m revenue overspend for 2026-27 must be funded from reserves. General Fund reserves are forecast to move from -£66.0m to -£84.8m, representing 5.1% of the net revenue budget (£1,655.6m). This comprises: repayment of previous overspend drawdown (£20.2m), rebuilding contribution (£16.8m), and current year overspend drawdown (£21.4m). The council's stated minimum target is 5% of net revenue budget.
findings.matters: Drawing down reserves to fund operational overspend weakens financial resilience and increases future replenishment requirements. At the minimum threshold with no buffer, any further adverse variance will cause the reserve to fall below policy minimum.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve opening balance -£66.0m, forecast closing -£84.8m (5.1% of £1,655.6m net revenue budget), in-year overspend funded from reserves £21.4m.
findings.quote: When the council overspends, it must fund that overspend from reserves. Any overspend is a concern for the authority and presents a risk to the Council's future financial sustainability and it is essential that the need to drawdown from reserves is reduced as far as possible, as drawdowns from reserves weaken the Council's financial resilience and increase the requirement to replenish reserves in future years.

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: £4.1m of planned savings for 2026-27 are undeliverable; £5.1m delayed to future years.
findings.detail: Of the £91.7m gross savings target for 2026-27, the council forecasts delivery of only £82.5m (90%). Of the £9.2m shortfall, £4.1m is identified as undeliverable (will not be achieved). Key undeliverable items: £2.0m Adult Social Care commissioning (new contract mobilization delayed to Q2/3), £0.7m legal savings (dependent on Courts speeding up proceedings, deemed unlikely), £0.6m contingent on Government actions on residential care costs. A further £5.1m of planned savings will now be delivered in future years instead.
findings.matters: Undeliverable savings indicate structural overspend: the underlying cost base is higher than planned. Savings targets of this scale not materializing suggest either the plans were over-ambitious or delivery capability is constrained. This implies future-year budgets face similar slippage risk.
findings.figures: Savings target £91.7m, forecast delivery £82.5m (90%), undeliverable £4.1m, delayed to future years £5.1m.
findings.quote: As at Quarter 1, £82.5m is expected to be delivered in 2026-27, which represents 90% delivery against the target. £9.2m of savings are currently not expected to be delivered in 2026-27. Of this amount, £5.1m is planned to be delivered in future financial years, with the remaining £4.1m no longer deliverable.

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: Looked After Children numbers rising 5% (70 more children); residential care costs up 23% year-on-year.
findings.detail: The number of Looked After Children has increased by 70 (5%) in the past year, with cost pressures driven by a shift from in-house foster care (declining capacity) to more expensive external market placements. Residential care costs have risen 23% between March 2025 and March 2026. This is generating a permanent forecast overspend of £16.8m for 2026-27, with a further £2.5m contingency for possible additional increases in numbers and costs. Mitigation through opening of four new in-house residential homes is slipping, with two homes now due to open later than planned, reducing expected savings by nearly £1m.
findings.matters: Demand-driven and cost-pressured. A 5% volume increase plus 23% price inflation on a service that is difficult to control represents structural, recurring financial pressure. The forecast shows mitigation plans slipping, with no certainty of future cost stabilization.
findings.figures: 70 additional LAC (5% year-on-year increase), residential care costs increased 23% between March 2025 and March 2026, forecast overspend £16.8m plus £2.5m contingency.
findings.quote: Historically the number of Looked After Children (LAC) has remained relatively steady but the number has started to rise since the last quarter of 2025-26, with 70 more children than a year ago (5% increase).

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: Schools DSG deficit forecast to increase to £238.5m; £162.5m government grant depends on DfE approval of reform plan not yet received.
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is forecast to increase from £130.5m to £238.5m in 2026-27. This is dependent on approval of a High Needs Stability Grant of £162.5m, which the council applied for in June 2026 and has not yet received. The statutory override allowing councils to hold DSG deficits separate from general reserves expires 31 March 2028. From 2028-29 onwards, the government has only stated an intention (not a guarantee) that councils will not be required to fund DSG deficits from the General Fund.
findings.matters: A £238.5m DSG deficit is a material financial liability. The funding solution depends entirely on government approval of an outcome still being determined. Once the statutory override ends in 15 months, the council faces funding uncertainty for the remaining deficit.
findings.figures: DSG deficit forecast £238.5m (from £130.5m opening), High Needs Stability Grant expected £162.5m (not approved), High Needs Block in-year overspend £109.2m, statutory override expires 31 March 2028.
findings.quote: This forecast position does not include the impact of the new High Needs Stability Grant, announced in February 2026, which depends on the Department for Education (DfE) approving a local Special Educational Needs & Disability (SEND) reform plan.

findings.headline: Information Commissioner's Office monitoring KCC performance on data subject access requests, with compliance at 57% vs 90% target
findings.detail: Subject Access Request (SAR) compliance was 57% (target 90%, floor 85%) — RED. The report states "The Information Commissioner's Office continues to monitor KCC's performance." 77% of requests come from the Children, Young People and Education Directorate, with SEN the main source of overdue cases. Performance declined for the second quarter in a row but is similar to the same quarter last year.
findings.matters: ICO monitoring is a formal compliance risk. Sustained non-compliance with statutory data protection timescales creates legal and reputational exposure. The concentration in SEN suggests EHCP-related cases are driving the backlog.
findings.figures: 57% within timescale vs 90% target (floor 85%); 77% of requests from CYPE; majority overdue relate to SEN.
findings.quote: For Subject Access Requests (SARs), performance decreased for the second quarter in a row, but is similar to the same quarter last year... The Information Commissioner's Office continues to monitor KCC's performance.

findings.headline: NHS Health Checks delivery collapsed 20% in quarter, missing target by 74% due to provider transition issues
findings.detail: Only 4,677 NHS Health Checks were delivered in Q1 against a target of 31,000 (15% of target; floor 24,800). This represents a 20% drop from the previous quarter (5,831). The report attributes the failure to "service changes, including the transition to new provider arrangements." No forward recovery plan is outlined. This is a mandated public health function.
findings.matters: A 74% miss against target on a preventive health programme suggests the provider transition was poorly managed or under-resourced. The scale of the shortfall indicates either service capacity was overstated or transition planning was inadequate.
findings.figures: 4,677 delivered vs 31,000 target (15% achievement); 24,800 floor; down from 5,831 previous quarter (20% decline).
findings.quote: Delivery of NHS Health Checks was significantly affected during this quarter by a number of service changes, including the transition to new provider arrangements.

findings.headline: Border resilience risk escalated to High on confirmation that EU and France will not pause checks, with infrastructure implications
findings.detail: Corporate Risk CRR0042 (Border fluidity, infrastructure and resilience) was escalated from Medium (15) to High (20) on 16 July 2026. The escalation followed "confirmation being received from the EU and France that there is no flexibility in temporarily pausing border checks." The implications for Kent, given Dover's position as England's primary freight gateway and Sevington Inland Border Facility throughput, include sustained congestion pressure, potential revenue impact on transport/parking services, and ongoing operational strain on council-coordinated responses.
findings.matters: A formal risk escalation affecting a strategic asset (Kent's border infrastructure) signals the council now faces sustained operational pressure in this area with no policy relief available. This can create unfunded cost pressures and affect revenue streams from services dependent on fluid border movement.
findings.figures: Risk escalation: Medium (score 15) to High (score 20); confirmed on 16/07/2026; no flexibility available from EU/France.
findings.quote: RISK RATING INCREASED: CRR0042 Border fluidity, infrastructure and resilience – Increased on 16/07/26 from Medium (15) to High (20) due to confirmation being received from the EU and France that there is no flexibility in temporarily pausing border checks.

findings.headline: Procurement 'savings' of £32.9m claimed but 75% are non-cashable cost avoidance, mostly from one-off highways contract
findings.detail: The council reports £32.9m in financial benefits, with £23.5m (71.5%) from the new Highway Term Maintenance Contract. However, the report explicitly states "the majority of financial benefits are categorised as cost avoidance, totalling £24.73m. This reflects the role of procurement activity in avoiding higher costs through effective tendering... However, these financial benefits should be distinguished from immediate cashable budget reductions." The £8m HTMC saving came from negotiation reducing tendered rates by 22%. The report cautions this is "exceptional" performance and the quarter "should be treated as exceptional reporting rather than requiring an adjustment of targets."
findings.matters: A headline 'savings' figure of £32.9m cannot be used to offset overspends or released to the budget — 75% is unrealised cost avoidance. The one-off nature and contractor-specific scale makes it unavailable for forward financial planning.
findings.figures: £32.9m total; £23.5m HTMC (71%); £24.73m cost avoidance (75%); HTMC delivery includes £8m negotiation on initial tender.
findings.quote: The majority of financial benefits are categorised as cost avoidance, totalling £24.73m. This reflects the role of procurement activity in avoiding higher costs through effective tendering, negotiation and challenge of pricing. However, these financial benefits should be distinguished from immediate cashable budget reductions. As a result, the quarter should be treated as exceptional reporting quarter, rather than requiring an adjustment of targets.

findings.headline: Developer contributions at highest level in 32 months, bringing £71.4m of capital funding for growth infrastructure
findings.detail: S106 contributions secured totalled £71.4m in Q1, representing 99.97% of amounts sought and the highest figure since December 2023. Contributions were concentrated in two major Thanet developments: £40.3m from a 1,600-dwelling scheme at Birchington (including £20.95m highways, £18.67m education) and £28.2m from 1,461-dwelling scheme at Margate (£19.63m education, £7.98m highways). The council achieved a 99.97% success rate against originally requested amounts.
findings.matters: Substantial incoming capital funding locked in for council infrastructure investment. A funding source that is predictable and now demonstrating strong collection suggests the council's ability to deliver growth-related capital schemes without increasing borrowing.
findings.figures: £71.4m total; £40.3m Birchington (1,600 dwellings); £28.2m Margate (1,461 dwellings); 99.97% success rate against amounts sought.
findings.quote: A total of £71.4m in contributions was secured this quarter, representing the highest figure since December 2023. This significant increase is largely attributable to two strategic developments granted planning permission in the Thanet district.

findings.headline: New highways contractor transition has introduced data system failures and service performance collapse on emergency response
findings.detail: Following transition to Ringway as the new Highway Term Maintenance Contract (HTMC) provider in May 2026, emergency incident response fell to 73% of target (89% in April under previous provider Amey). The report states: "Issues have been identified with the reporting systems and the configuration of data transfers between systems, which are affecting the accuracy of performance reporting. As a result, the underlying data and reporting outputs are currently being jointly investigated by KCC and Ringway." Routine enquiry response is also RED at 73%.
findings.matters: A major outsourced service shows both operational failure (emergency response) and data integrity failure (unable to reliably report performance). Both create immediate service risk and prevent accurate monitoring of contractor delivery.
findings.figures: Emergency incidents: 73% actual vs 98% target (floor 95%); April performance under Amey: 89%; routine enquiries: 73% vs 90% target.
findings.quote: Issues have been identified with the reporting systems and the configuration of data transfers between systems, which are affecting the accuracy of performance reporting. As a result, the underlying data and reporting outputs are currently being jointly investigated by KCC and Ringway to establish an agreed and validated performance position, to ensure accurate reporting of data.

findings.headline: Children's services staffing fell 5.2 percentage points in quarter, dropping to 82.6% of target and increasing reliance on agency spend
findings.detail: Percentage of the case-holding establishment with staff in post fell from 87.8% to 82.6%, a decline of 5.2pp and below the 90% target. This is the second consecutive quarter of decline and sits just 2.6pp above the 80% floor. The report does not provide forward staffing plans.
findings.matters: Persistent staffing shortfalls typically drive higher-cost agency engagement, increase service quality risk, and create budget volatility. A 5.2pp quarterly drop signals deteriorating recruitment or retention.
findings.figures: 82.6% current vs 87.8% previous quarter; 2.4pp above floor of 80%; target 90%.
findings.quote: Percentage of the case-holding establishment with a member of staff present in post AMBER. Latest: 82.6% Target: 90%, Floor 80% Previous: 87.8%

findings.headline: Safeguarding caseload at highest level in 18 months, signalling rising demand and forward cost pressure
findings.detail: Open safeguarding work increased from 2,418 to 2,881 in Quarter 1, described as "highest level since Quarter 3, 2024/25." This tracks a pattern of rising incoming concerns: 6,029 received this quarter, up from 5,796 in the previous quarter. The report attributes some increase to "hot weather" but notes the broader trend has been upward.
findings.matters: Growing safeguarding caseload creates forward pressure on staffing budgets and service costs. Unmet caseload growth is an early warning of future spending needs or service quality deterioration.
findings.figures: 2,881 open cases; up from 2,418 previous quarter (19% increase); up from lowest level of 2,418 in Quarter 4 2024/25; 6,029 concerns received vs 5,796 previous quarter.
findings.quote: Open work is at its highest level since Quarter 3, 2024/25. In Quarter 1, the amount of open work increased from 2,418 to 2,881, this will be a mixture of ongoing enquiries and incoming concerns that are being triaged.

findings.headline: Adult social care residential admissions now exceed a newly lowered target, signalling demand pressure despite tightened expectations
findings.detail: Admissions to residential and nursing care for adults aged 65+ reached 576 per 100,000 (rolling 12-month), measured against a new target of 515 — down from 588 in the previous year. Despite the lower threshold, performance is RED. The report notes "the target for this measure has changed for this financial year" and is "based on performance in 2024/25," indicating the council set a tighter benchmark it has failed to meet.
findings.matters: The council has explicitly tightened its admission target yet still overshot it. This signals underlying demand pressures that the authority cannot contain and suggests structural spending above its own revised tolerance.
findings.figures: 576 actual vs 515 target (floor 560); change from 588 to 515 target year-on-year represents a 12% reduction in acceptable admissions but actual performance did not improve.
findings.quote: Long Term support needs of older people (65 and over) met by admission to residential and nursing care homes, per 100,000 – rolling 12 months. Latest: 576 Target: 515, Floor: 560 Previous: 584 (Green). The target for this measure has changed for this financial year, moving from 588 to 515.

findings.headline: SEND placement costs rising as new special schools remain delayed, forcing greater reliance on expensive independent provision
findings.detail: 10.8% of pupils with EHCPs are placed in independent or out-of-county special schools against a target of 9%. The report attributes this to "delayed provision of two new special schools, leading to a continued over-reliance on independent specialist provision to compensate." Despite recent DfE assurance that the schools remain in their plans, the report states this "is likely to remain below target for the foreseeable future."
findings.matters: Direct and ongoing budget pressure: independent school fees are substantially higher than maintained provision. Delayed capital delivery is forcing sustained overspend on recurrent costs.
findings.figures: 10.8% vs target 9.0%; KCC is 0.8 percentage points above tolerance and acknowledges ongoing pressure from new school approvals in the independent sector.
findings.quote: The percentage of pupils with EHCPs being placed in independent or out of county special schools, at 10.8%, remains higher than the target of 9.0%. As previously reported, Kent continues to feel the effect of the delayed provision of two new special schools, leading to a continued over-reliance on independent specialist provision to compensate.

findings.headline: Capital spending includes a £35.2m rephasing variance, indicating project deferrals.
findings.detail: The capital forecast outturn shows a £32m total underspend split between a £3.1m real underspend and a -£35.2m rephasing variance. The significant rephasing element indicates £35.2m of budgeted capital projects are being deferred into future financial years.
findings.matters: Large capital rephasing affects the council's multi-year borrowing requirements and may indicate delivery constraints or scheme viability concerns that affect capital programme credibility.
findings.figures: £32m underspend; £3.1m real variance; -£35.2m rephasing variance
findings.quote: The capital forecast outturn position is a £32m underspend against budget, split between a £3.1m real variance and a -£35.2m rephasing variance.

findings.headline: Kent is forecasting a £21.4m revenue overspend in 2026-27, representing 1.3% of the overall budget.
findings.detail: In Q1 monitoring, the Council reports a revenue forecast outturn variance of £21.4m overspend against budget. This indicates the Council is running ahead of budget in the opening quarter of the financial year, requiring either corrective action or explanation of how the overspend will be managed.
findings.matters: A material Q1 overspend suggests the council may struggle to deliver its full-year budget and raises questions about spend control and reserves sustainability.
findings.figures: £21.4m overspend; 1.3% of overall budget
findings.quote: The forecast outturn variance against the revenue budget is an overspend of £21.4m, which represents 1.3% of the overall budget.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Fund administration faces staffing shortages affecting operational capacity.
findings.detail: Administration staffing was underspent (budget £3.455m, actual £3.382m) not through cost control but because vacancies were unfilled or filled from internal candidates, leaving 'backfill vacancies outstanding'. This indicates recruitment and retention challenges within the administration team.
findings.matters: Understaffing in pension administration increases operational risk, processing delays, and error potential; combined with the data quality issues reported separately, it suggests the team is under resource pressure.
findings.figures: Administration staffing budget: £3.455m; actual: £3.382m (underspent £73k)
findings.quote: Administration staffing costs had an underspend due to the budget being set anticipating vacancies being filled. However, where recruitment campaigns have been completed and vacancies filled, some have come from internal candidates which leave backfill vacancies outstanding.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Pension data rectification project faces delays due to system access issues.
findings.detail: The multi-year data rectification project, budgeted at £2.012m, incurred only £1.020m in 2025-26. The underspend reflects delays rather than savings: 'Progress has been impacted by issues relating to system access and ensuring accurate data has been received from employers.' The project is required for Pensions Dashboard compliance.
findings.matters: Data quality problems in pension administration suggest underlying IT or operational weaknesses; failure to complete the project and meet the Dashboard deadline could result in regulatory penalties.
findings.figures: Data rectification project budget £2.012m; actual spend £1.020m; shortfall £991k
findings.quote: The data rectification project is a multi-year exercise and is progressing, but the invoicing is dependent on progress being made. Progress has been impacted by issues relating to system access and ensuring accurate data has been received from employers.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation poses unprecedented structural risk to the fund.
findings.detail: The Fund Chairman identifies LGR as 'one of the most consequential developments facing the Fund', noting it will have 'important implications for governance, employer participation, administration and member services'. The Fund is engaged in cross-authority project work to assess impact and determine future host authority arrangements, but outcomes remain uncertain.
findings.matters: Major local government reorganisation could reshape the fund's employer base, governance structure, and financial position; this represents material risk to both Kent County Council and its credit position.
findings.figures: 265 active employers (down from 272 in prior year); 185,028 total fund members
findings.quote: Looking ahead, one of the most consequential developments facing the Fund is Local Government Reorganisation. The scale of change proposed across local government is unprecedented and will have important implications for governance, employer participation, administration and member services.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Fund assets increased by almost £1bn to £9.4bn, driven by strong investment returns.
findings.detail: Net fund assets grew from £8.451bn to £9.418bn, an increase of £966.7m. Investment performance delivered 11.5% return, outperforming the benchmark of 10.8%, occurring despite pausing certain asset transitions pending completion of the move to Border to Coast Pensions Partnership.
findings.matters: A growing fund improves the council's pension position, reduces the risk of future contribution increases, and indicates effective investment management through a period of governance transition.
findings.figures: Fund value 2024-25: £8.451bn; 2025-26: £9.418bn; increase £966.7m; investment return 11.5% vs benchmark 10.8%
findings.quote: Investment assets have continued to grow in value in a supportive investment environment, taking the Fund from £8.45bn in 2024/25, to £9.42bn in 2025/26, an increase of almost £1bn.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Fund management and administration costs jumped 39% in one year.
findings.detail: Total costs (administration, governance, and investment management) increased from £40.1m to £55.8m, a jump of £15.7m. Fund manager fees alone increased approximately £2.5m due to higher asset valuations and fee structures; additional significant costs came from property acquisition transactions undertaken to rebalance the portfolio.
findings.matters: Rapidly escalating administrative costs reduce the net benefit to the fund and employers; a lender would want to understand whether this cost inflation is permanent and sustainable.
findings.quote: Fund manager fees have increased by roughly £2.5m when compared to the budget. This is as a result of forecasts being set on estimate valuations set 12 months in advance. In this case, those valuations had grown at a quicker pace than forecast, especially in the equities asset class which is very volatile. As fees are paid on the value of asset under management, this has led to an increase in fees.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Pension benefit payments are growing much faster than contribution income.
findings.detail: Annual benefit payments increased 6.3% in the year to £353.5m, outpacing contribution growth. Over five years, benefits have grown 37% while pensioner numbers have risen 18%, showing the fund is in a paying-out phase with more retirees and fewer working members proportionally.
findings.matters: Although the fund is currently 104% funded, this structural imbalance means long-term sustainability depends on sustained investment returns; a significant market downturn could quickly reverse the surplus and force higher employer contributions.
findings.quote: The amount the Fund spends on benefits has increased by 6.3% over the year, which was slightly above the increase in contribution income, and by 37% since 2021/22.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Pension fund improved to 104% funded; employers will pay lower contribution rates.
findings.detail: The triennial valuation as at 31 March 2025 shows the fund's funding level improved from 102% to 104%. This improvement resulted in lower contribution rates for the majority of participating employers, explicitly described as 'particularly welcome at a time when many local authorities and public sector bodies continue to face significant financial challenges'.
findings.matters: Lower pension contribution rates ease pressure on the council's revenue budget at a time of financial strain; this improves the council's ability to fund other services and remain solvent.
findings.figures: Funding level: 102% (2025 valuation) to 104% (2026 valuation); contribution rates lower for majority of employers
findings.quote: the valuation resulted in lower contribution rates for the majority of participating employers. This was particularly welcome at a time when many local authorities and public sector bodies continue to face significant financial challenges.

findings.headline: Pension aggregation case processing quality fell sharply to 32.3% in June
findings.detail: Aggregation actual cases KPI performance declined from 75% in April to 32.3% in June, a 43-percentage-point drop over two months. The intermediate May figure of 64.7% suggests consistent deterioration through the quarter.
findings.matters: Significant declines in pension processing KPIs could indicate capacity shortages, control failures, or systemic issues that might delay member benefits and trigger regulatory concerns.
findings.figures: Aggregation actuals KPI: April 75%, May 64.7%, June 32.3%
findings.quote: Aggregation actuals 4 75 17 64.7 62 32.3

findings.headline: Pension scheme data quality improved from below to above regulatory compliance standard
findings.detail: Scheme-specific data quality as measured by TPR (The Pensions Regulator) pass rate improved from 83.15% in Q4 2025-26 to 97.95% in Q2 2026. This indicates resolution of a regulatory data quality issue that had previously been below acceptable compliance levels.
findings.matters: Regulatory data quality compliance is a prerequisite for unqualified pension scheme operation; movement from below-compliance to compliance indicates remediation of a governance weakness.
findings.figures: Scheme Specific TPR Pass Rate: 83.15% (Jan-Mar 2026) to 97.95% (Apr-Jun 2026)
findings.quote: Scheme Specific 83.15 97.95

findings.headline: Administration staff budget running £155,098 under budget while most other cost lines overspend.
findings.detail: Against a budgeted administration payroll of £4,296,332, the forecast shows spend of only £4,141,234. This is the largest single saving in the forecast and partially offsets widespread overspends elsewhere. The underspend may indicate staff vacancies or turnover not yet filled.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to understand whether staffing savings are planned or incidental to their forecasting, as sustained vacancies can either represent genuine savings or risk to service delivery and future recruitment costs.
findings.figures: Administration Staff budget £4,296,332; forecast £4,141,234; underspend £155,098
findings.quote: Administration Staff 4,296,332 4,141,234 155,098

findings.headline: Pension fund administration forecast shows £233,260 overspend in Q1, with staff underspend offset by operational cost overruns.
findings.detail: The Q1 forecast projects total administration costs of £59,647,422 against a budget of £59,414,162. A £155,098 underspend in administration staff is more than offset by overspends across multiple operational areas: IT expenses £152,644 over budget, printing and mailing costs £69,648 over, KCC overhead recharges £50,902 over, and pooling costs £37,900 over, among others.
findings.matters: Finance directors track all budgets including pension fund administration as part of overall financial control. Early Q1 overspends across multiple cost areas suggest operational pressures that, if sustained, would accumulate to roughly £900,000 for a full financial year (on a £59.4m budget).
findings.figures: Total overspend £233,260; Administration Staff underspend £155,098; IT Expenses overspend £152,644; Printing and Mailing overspend £69,648; KCC Overheads overspend £50,902; Pooling Costs overspend £37,900

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Full Year Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: IFRS 9 statutory override expires in 2029, exposing the council's revenue budget to future volatility from pooled fund investments.
findings.detail: The IFRS 9 statutory override that currently shields the council's revenue budget from fair value movements in pooled fund investments expires on 31 March 2029. From 2029-30 onwards, movements in the £186.6m pooled fund portfolio will flow through the revenue account. The council has already recognised this risk on its Budget Risk Register and commenced a strategy to reduce pooled fund holdings.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand future revenue budget volatility. When the override expires, investment losses will directly impact the council's annual revenue outturn, potentially requiring budget adjustments or reserve drawdowns to manage volatility.
findings.figures: £186.6m in pooled fund investments; override expires 31 March 2029; council redeeming holdings from CCLA Property Fund
findings.quote: Given the uncertainty surrounding the impact of the expiry of the override, the Council recogises this risk on the Budget Risk Register.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Full Year Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Liquid cash reserves fell below the council's minimum prudent threshold at year-end due to early debt repayment.
findings.detail: At 31 March 2026, cash available within 3 months was £71.3m, falling marginally below the council's minimum prudent threshold of £75m. This occurred because of early repayment of £90m in loans undertaken to reduce interest costs. The council states this was temporary, with balances recovering to £118m by 30 June 2026.
findings.matters: Lenders monitor whether councils maintain adequate liquidity buffers. A breach of the council's own control indicators—even if temporary—shows that treasury decisions can tighten near-term cash positions beyond planned minimums, signalling execution risk.
findings.figures: Cash available within 3 months: £71.3m (actual) vs £75m (minimum); early repayment totalling £90m
findings.quote: Liquid cash levels dropped marginally below the minimum level for a short period of time due to early debt repayment.

findings.paper_title: Budget Planning Process 2027-28 and MTFP Update Report
findings.headline: Policy to minimise one-off solutions for 2027-28 despite widening gap signals structural balance challenge
findings.detail: The paper explicitly states reliance on one-off measures (capital receipts flexibility, reserve drawdowns) should be minimised and only a last resort for 2027-28, to avoid burdening successor authorities post-reorganisation. This policy choice in a year with increasing deficits indicates the council anticipates difficulty achieving sustainable recurring balance.
findings.matters: Voluntary policy restricting one-off financing options ahead of a widening gap suggests structural pressure exceeds cyclical pressure; council is pre-committing to harder permanent spending decisions.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Reliance on one-off measures to achieve a balanced budget for 2027-28 should be minimised and only considered as a last resort as otherwise this would leave a legacy replacement issue post LGR.

findings.paper_title: Budget Planning Process 2027-28 and MTFP Update Report
findings.headline: Capital programme sharply constrained ahead of local government reorganisation; new projects excluded to avoid abortive spend burdening successor councils
findings.detail: Kent's local government reorganisation means the council is explicitly limiting capital spending to avoid projects that successor authorities may not continue, as these would create revenue pressure on new councils. New capital bids are limited to projects that are fully funded or invest-to-save only; forward analysis of potential projects is no longer included.
findings.matters: Reduced capital investment in the transitional year signals constrained asset maintenance and improvement capacity; postponed capital schemes may create legacy issues for successor councils that reduce their financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: It is particularly important that the Council does not incur capital costs on projects that may not be continued by new authorities as otherwise this could result in significant abortive costs which would represent a revenue pressure on the new councils. In light of LGR it is proposed the analysis of potential projects is no longer included in the plans for 2027-28.

findings.paper_title: Budget Planning Process 2027-28 and MTFP Update Report
findings.headline: Adult social care strategy relies on ambitious fee cap and contract retendering with acknowledged risk of legal challenge
findings.detail: Adult social care strategy includes limiting fee uplifts to affordable levels and retendering contracts to add new providers, alongside review of self-funded costs. The paper explicitly acknowledges this approach carries "significant risks, not least an ambitious programme for retendering contracts and risks of legal challenge".
findings.matters: Legal challenges to fee negotiations could force upward payment revision and negate planned savings; contract retendering failures would leave placement costs uncontrolled.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: In adopting this strategy, it was recognised this came with significant risks, not least an ambitious programme for retendering contracts and risks of legal challenge.

findings.paper_title: Budget Planning Process 2027-28 and MTFP Update Report
findings.headline: Forecast deficit gap is widening but savings solutions remain unidentified at time of this paper
findings.detail: The initial forecast update expected to show a larger gap between resources and spending needs, therefore raising required savings. However, savings options have not yet been developed; they will be worked up only in subsequent months after this forecast is finalised.
findings.matters: A widening deficit with savings still unidentified creates execution risk and signals the council anticipates real constraint beyond routine efficiency gains.
findings.figures: Gap size to be updated in autumn; specific savings unidentified
findings.quote: These are likely to increase the gap (and therefore savings requirement). Savings options will then be developed ahead of the autumn update.

findings.paper_title: Budget Planning Process 2027-28 and MTFP Update Report
findings.headline: Inflation shock from Middle East energy crisis adds 1-4% to forecasts, equivalent to £10m per 1% variance against plan
findings.detail: Bank of England's April 2026 monetary policy update revised inflation forecasts upward by 1-4% above the November OBR assumptions that underpinned the existing MTFP. The council explicitly quantifies the impact: each 1% variance above current forecast creates £10m additional budget pressure.
findings.matters: Unforecasted inflation erodes the financial assumptions on which borrowing capacity and financial viability are based, forcing either discretionary spending cuts or use of reserves.
findings.figures: Inflation now forecast 1% to 4% higher than November OBR forecast; each 1% above current MTFP adds circa £10m
findings.quote: Following the conflict inflation is now forecast to be between 1% to 4% higher in 2026 than the November OBR forecast. Each 1% above the current MTFP forecast adds circa £10m to the Council's budget pressures

findings.paper_title: 26-00030 - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report – Outturn 2025-2026
findings.headline: Early repayment of £50m debt in September 2025-26 reduced investment income and cash balances, signalling a shift from the stated borrowing strategy.
findings.detail: The council received £52m upfront Highways Maintenance grant and used it to early-repay £50m debt in September 2025-26. This saved borrowing costs but reduced investment income and cash balances fell £159.9m to £315.9m. The paper notes investment income forecast is 'quite volatile' depending on timing of receipts and repayments.
findings.matters: Early repayment reduces future interest costs but also reduces liquidity and investment income. Combined with reserves at the 5% threshold, this limits the council's financial flexibility for unexpected costs or slower savings delivery.
findings.figures: Early debt repayment £50m (September 2025-26); cash balances fell £159.9m to £315.9m; Highways grant received upfront £52m
findings.quote: The reduction in investment income as a result of the lower cash balances following the early debt repayment is more than offset by the discount and interest saved from repaying the loan early. The reported underspend also reflects savings in borrowing costs due to early repayment of a loan at the end of 2024-25 and another at the end of 2025-26.

findings.paper_title: 26-00030 - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report – Outturn 2025-2026
findings.headline: Savings targets of £121.5m were only 81% delivered (£98.6m achieved), with £13.3m undelivered rolled to 2026-27, signalling systematic failure to hit efficiency plans.
findings.detail: The council's 2025-26 savings requirement was £121.5m (£99.0m in-year plus £22.5m carried from 2024-25). Actual delivery was £98.6m, leaving £22.9m unmet. Of this, £13.3m rolled into 2026-27 budgets. Adult Social Care alone underdelivered by £20.7m, and other major savings (HR spans/layers £0.5m, procurement-related items) fell short.
findings.matters: Consistent 18%+ shortfall on savings targets means the council is relying on reserves and contingency underspends elsewhere to balance the budget, creating structural funding pressure.
findings.figures: 2025-26 savings target £121.5m; achievement £98.6m; shortfall £22.9m; ASCH underdelivery £20.7m; HR spans/layers saving undeliverable £0.5m
findings.quote: In total, £98.6m of savings and additional income was achieved in 2025-26, including £3.3m of alternative savings identified and delivered compared to the original planned saving. £13.3m of the undelivered savings are expected to be achieved in future years and have been rolled into the 2026-27 budget.

findings.paper_title: 26-00030 - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report – Outturn 2025-2026
findings.headline: General Fund reserves fell to approximately 4.3% of budget after funding £22.7m overspend, below the stated 5% target, and forecast recovery assumes no future drawdowns.
findings.detail: The council held a General Fund reserve of £66.0m at 31 March 2026 after drawing down £22.7m to cover the overspend. This represents approximately 4.3% of the £1,531.9m net revenue budget (below the 5% target). Recovery to 6% by 2027-28 assumes 'no drawdowns are required to fund overspending in future years' — a condition that may not hold given identified ASCH and DSG pressures.
findings.matters: Reserves at or below 5% leave limited buffer for unexpected pressures or savings shortfalls. If ASCH and DSG pressures continue, the council risks reserves falling dangerously low.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve £66.0m (approx 4.3% of net revenue budget); budget requires 5% minimum; forecast recovery to 6% in 2026-27 'assuming no drawdowns'
findings.quote: General Reserves will be below 5% of the 2025-6 net revenue budget as at 31 March 2026 after funding the in-year revenue overspend. However, once budgeted contributions are made as per the Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP), and assuming no drawdowns are required to fund overspending in future years, the percentage is forecasted to be above 6% in 2026-27.

findings.paper_title: 26-00030 - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report – Outturn 2025-2026
findings.headline: Looked After Children placement costs rose 23% year-on-year, with the service shifting from in-house to external provision and now overspending by £13.7m.
findings.detail: The 'Looked After Children - Care and Support (Placements)' overspend of £13.7m is driven by 'faster-than-expected reductions in in-house foster placements and greater reliance on external provision, including IFAs and residential care.' Residential care costs specifically rose 23% (Mar 2025–Mar 2026). One high-needs child accounts for £2.4m of disabled LAC spend.
findings.matters: A 23% year-on-year rise in placement costs, combined with a shift to more expensive external provision, creates a rapidly compounding budget pressure that is hard to reverse without major service redesign or procurement savings.
findings.figures: Looked After Children overspend £13.7m; residential care costs rose 23% (Mar 2025–Mar 2026); one high-needs child accounts for £2.4m
findings.quote: This overspend is driven by faster-than-expected reductions in in-house foster placements and greater reliance on external provision, including IFAs and residential care. Health contributions have fallen by £1.4m, while residential care costs rose 23% (Mar 2025–Mar 2026).

findings.paper_title: 26-00030 - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report – Outturn 2025-2026
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspent by £42.9m, with half the overspend coming from failure to deliver planned savings, while costs and demand continue rising.
findings.detail: ASCH was the largest overspend directorate. Of the £42.9m overspend, £20.7m relates to non-delivery of in-year savings. The remainder is driven by higher costs for placements and inflationary pressures on provider fees. Older People Residential Care alone overspent by £25.4m (£19.8m from higher demand, £6.9m from unmet savings).
findings.matters: A £42.9m recurrent overspend in a service with modest demand growth signals that unit costs are rising faster than budgeted and that planned efficiency savings are not being achieved, creating a structural gap.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care overspend £42.9m; unachieved savings £20.7m; Older People Residential Care overspend £25.4m
findings.quote: Approaching 50% of the ASCH overspend relates to non-delivery of savings, however much of this has been identified as achievable in future years. The remainder is largely driven by increases in costs (both complexity and inflationary) to deliver social care placements from providers.

findings.paper_title: 26-00030 - Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report – Outturn 2025-2026
findings.headline: Schools' Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has grown to £130.5m and is forecast to worsen to £100m+ annual shortfalls despite government reform commitment.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit grew from £97.5m opening balance to £130.5m closing. The High Needs Block overspent by £64.6m in-year due to higher demand for SEND and more expensive specialist provision. The council no longer expects breakeven by 2027-28. Future deficits depend on government accepting the council's SEN reform plan to release the High Needs Stability Grant (estimated £162.5m, subject to DfE approval).
findings.matters: A £130.5m deficit on a statutory grant is the council's single largest financial risk and creates unpredictable future drawdowns on the general fund if government reform doesn't materialise as planned.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £130.5m (up from £97.5m opening); High Needs Block overspend £64.6m; forecast annual shortfalls 2026-27 and 2027-28 of over £100m per year
findings.quote: The Council no longer expects to reach an in-year breakeven position by 2027-28, with estimated annual shortfalls in 2026-27 and 2027-28 of over £100m per year, acerbated by the high needs grant being frozen at 2025-26 levels with no increase for inflation or demand pressures.

findings.paper_title: Public Report - Local Government Re-organisation and Kent Pension Fund
findings.headline: Analysis of new Single Purpose Pension Authority option proceeding with South Yorkshire precedent
findings.detail: A new Kent Single Purpose Pension Authority (SPPA) is one of five options being evaluated. The South Yorkshire Pensions Authority is cited as the only existing true LGPS single-purpose authority (created 1986 when South Yorkshire MCC was abolished), governed by twelve councillors and funded entirely from the pension fund apart from unfunded pension payments recharged to district councils.
findings.matters: If the SPPA option is selected, it would require creating a new entity with its own governance structure and funding model, distinct from normal council operations. This has structural and cost implications that differ significantly from hosting within an existing authority.
findings.figures: South Yorkshire Pensions Authority is made up of twelve councillors drawn from the four metropolitan districts
findings.quote: A new Kent Single Purpose Pension Authority (SPPA) be created and designated as the AA for the Fund.

findings.paper_title: Public Report - Local Government Re-organisation and Kent Pension Fund
findings.headline: Kent Pension Fund administration must transfer to new host by 2028 due to council abolition
findings.detail: Kent County Council, the current administering authority for the Kent Pension Fund, will cease to exist following Local Government Reorganisation in 2028. A new host authority must be designated by the Secretary of State. This is a material structural change to pension fund governance that requires significant planning and coordination.
findings.matters: Pension fund administration is core to council financial stewardship; disruption or poor transition could affect member services, governance effectiveness, and ongoing costs. Finance directors and lenders care about whether critical functions are managed smoothly through structural change.
findings.figures: currently eighty-six bodies in England and Wales with the LGPS administering authority function
findings.quote: Following Local Government Reorganisation in 2028, Kent County Council will no longer exist, and a new host authority will need to be designated by the Secretary of State at the Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government (SoS).

findings.paper_title: Late changes to the 2026-27 Revenue Budget and 2026-2029 Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP)
findings.headline: A £183.5m medium-term High Needs (SEND) deficit remains unresolved despite new government grant
findings.detail: The council has overspent on SEND services since 2018, accumulating a £136.5m deficit. A new High Needs Stability Grant will cover 90% of this accumulated deficit, but £183.5m in total medium-term risk remains (including future deficits as SEND spending continues to exceed DSG funding). The paper identifies this as the council's most significant financial risk and on par with Adult Social Care pressures as material threats to financial sustainability.
findings.matters: An unresolved structural deficit of this magnitude indicates persistent mismatch between service demand and available funding that could materially impact creditworthiness and require future service cuts or general fund transfers.
findings.figures: Accumulated DSG deficit £136.485m; underlying deficit before Safety Valve contributions £296.985m; new grant £167.887m; total medium-term unresolved risk £183.5m (compared to previously identified risk of £238.5m)
findings.quote: These deficits are likely to still be significant with a net risk (DSG deficit less unapplied Stability Grant and new local SEND reserve) of £183.5m over the medium term. The £183.5m would still be the most significant item in the risk register and still means SEND deficit is on par with the Adult Social Care risks as the most material risks to the Council's continued financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Treasury investment balances declining 18% from £315m to £259m, reducing financial flexibility
findings.detail: The council's investment balances are forecast to decline from approximately £315m at the end of 2025-26 to £259m at the end of 2026-27—a reduction of about £56m. This reflects the council using its cash reserves to fund operations and capital expenditure, progressively reducing its available liquidity.
findings.matters: Declining reserves mean the council has less cash cushion to cover unexpected costs, revenue shortfalls, or to take advantage of opportunities. For a lender, this represents deteriorating financial flexibility and reduced capacity to absorb shocks.
findings.figures: £315m end 2025-26, £259m end 2026-27 (forecast). Earlier table shows Treasury investments of £287.2m (31.3.26) declining to £231.6m (31.3.27)
findings.quote: investment balances are forecast to be around £315m at the end of 2025-26 and approximately £259m at the end of 2026-27

findings.headline: £80m of LOBO loans have option dates during 2026-27, with lenders likely to exercise them
findings.detail: The council holds £90m of LOBO loans (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) where lenders can propose interest rate increases at set dates. The document explicitly states that £80m of these loans have option dates falling in 2026-27, and 'there is a reasonable chance that lenders will exercise their options.' If they do, the council must either accept new rates or find cash to repay the loans.
findings.matters: This is a forced refinancing event that could materially increase borrowing costs if lenders propose significantly higher rates, or require the council to find cash to repay rather than refinance.
findings.figures: £90m total LOBO loans, £80m with 2026-27 option dates. Current LOBO rate: 4.15%
findings.quote: LOBOs totalling £80m have option dates during 2026-27, and there is a reasonable chance that lenders will exercise their options. If they do, the Council will need to explore the option to repay LOBO loans to reduce refinancing risk in later years.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 External Audit Plan for Kent County Council
findings.headline: Change in asset revaluation method from annual revaluation to five-yearly with indexation in intervening years, effective 2025/26
findings.detail: From 2025/26, the Council must adopt a new CIPFA Code approach where Property, Plant and Equipment revaluations occur once every five years with indexation in intervening years, rather than annual revaluation. The audit identifies this as a substantial change requiring new valuation instructions, potential system changes, and asset record updates. It is flagged as a significant risk due to complexity and size of the balance sheet impact.
findings.matters: Land and building valuations are material estimates on the balance sheet and can be volatile. A change in valuation methodology creates risk of error or inconsistency. The audit notes this is 'a substantial change' and plans to engage its own valuation expert to challenge the Council's assumptions and index selections.
findings.figures: Applies to Property, Plant and Equipment; five-year rolling valuation cycle; change effective for first time in 2025/26
findings.quote: From 2025-26, in intervening years, current value will be updated using appropriate indexation, unless a desktop valuation is required due to absence of a suitable index. The Authority will adopt this approach for the first time in 2025-26, it is a substantial change to the accounting for non-current assets.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 External Audit Plan for Kent County Council
findings.headline: Significant governance changes since May 2025 Council elections create risk to effective decision-making
findings.detail: Since the May 2025 Council elections, there has been 'a number of significant changes in the administration's membership' in 'a relatively short period'. The audit has identified this as a risk of significant weakness in governance arrangements. The auditor plans to interview Members and officers to assess the robustness of decision-making.
findings.matters: A lender relies on Council leadership to make prudent financial decisions and manage risks. Rapid turnover in elected membership, particularly following an election, can mean loss of experience in complex financial governance, weaker challenge of management, and delayed decision-making during a period when the Council is facing material financial pressures.
findings.figures: Significant changes in administration membership since May 2025 elections
findings.quote: Since Council elections in May 2025 there has been a number of significant changes in the administration's membership. The number of changes, in a relatively short period, could have possible impacts to effective decision-making arrangements at the Council.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 External Audit Plan for Kent County Council
findings.headline: Oracle Fusion financial system went live in August 2025 in first year of operation with identified significant audit risk
findings.detail: The Council migrated its core financial system from Oracle EBS to Oracle Fusion in August 2025. The audit has identified this as a significant risk of material misstatement at financial statements level. The plan includes specialist IT audit work to verify data migration completeness and accuracy, and to assess control weaknesses in the new system. This is the first year operating the new system and there is heightened risk of control failures.
findings.matters: A lender and finance director need to have confidence that the financial statements for 2025/26 are reliable. A major system migration in the audit year creates material risk of data loss, account coding errors, or failed controls that go undetected. The audit acknowledges 'heightened risk of control weaknesses, configuration errors and instability of newly implemented processes'.
findings.figures: Migration completed August 2025; covers all financial reporting, expenditure, payables, payroll and journal entries
findings.quote: System migration can introduce inherent risks due to changes in financial reporting functionality, workflow configuration, access controls and the transfer of large volumes of financial data. Errors during data migration or new system configuration may result in incomplete, inaccurate or misstated financial balances in the 2025/26 financial statements. As this is the first year of operating the new system there is a heightened risk of control weaknesses, configuration errors and instability of newly implemented processes.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 External Audit Plan for Kent County Council
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget relies on planned drawdown of non-recurring reserves and capital receipts, not sustained savings
findings.detail: The S151 Officer's S25 report (issued February 2026) acknowledges that 2026/27 is balanced through one-off use of reserves and capital receipts. This is not sustainable. The same report recognises both the Adult Social Care and DSG pressures and the impact of the Council Tax flexibility decision.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council has a sustainable budget position. Balancing a budget with one-off reserves and asset sales (capital receipts) is a warning sign that structural spending exceeds recurring income and that reserves are being deployed to mask the problem.
findings.figures: 2026/27 balanced through reserves and capital receipts drawdown; these are explicitly identified as non-recurring
findings.quote: The S25 report, issued by the S151 Officer in February 2026 recognises the risks that the Council faces in the future, with 2026-27 being balanced through planned use of reserves and capital receipts, which are non-recurring.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 External Audit Plan for Kent County Council
findings.headline: Council foregoes £1 in Council Tax flexibility per 1% by setting 2026/27 budget increase at 3.99% instead of available 4.99%
findings.detail: The Council has chosen not to use the full Council Tax raising flexibility available to it under the government's council tax cap. The impact is a reduction in planned recurring revenue for 2026/27. The audit plan identifies this as creating a risk of significant weakness in arrangements for financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A lender sees this as a voluntary reduction in recurring revenue. It suggests either political preference for lower council tax over service investment, or an inability to justify additional income to residents. Either way, it reduces the financial headroom available to manage future overspends without reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Council Tax increase set at 3.99%, 1% below the 4.99% flexibility allowed
findings.quote: The Council has set a balanced budget for 2026/27 after foregoing full Council Tax flexibility, increasing council tax by 3.99%, 1% less than the total flexibility allowed.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 External Audit Plan for Kent County Council
findings.headline: DSG deficit for High Needs Block (SEND) reached £136.5m cumulatively, with a forecast £67.5m overspend in 2025/26 alone
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit, particularly in the High Needs Block for special education provision, has been a significant weakness since 2024/25. The cumulative deficit has grown to £136.5m. The audit plan identifies there is a risk that the significant weakness with regards to arrangements to mitigate the DSG deficit continue.
findings.matters: A growing DSG deficit of this magnitude represents a liability the council may struggle to repay. It signals failure to control special needs spending and suggests future years may require exceptional intervention or borrowing. It is material to overall financial sustainability and a key indicator of whether the council can maintain current service levels.
findings.figures: £67.5m forecast overspend in 2025/26; £136.5m cumulative DSG deficit
findings.quote: Significant financial challenges with regard to DSG continue, with a forecast DSG overspend of £67.5m in 2025/26, increasing the cumulative DSG deficit to £136.5m.

findings.paper_title: 2025/26 External Audit Plan for Kent County Council
findings.headline: Adult Social Care spending continues to exceed budget, with a forecast net overspend of £36.5m in 2025/26
findings.detail: Adult Social Care has been identified as a significant weakness in VFM arrangements since 2024/25 and remains unresolved. The Quarter 3 budget monitoring for 2025/26 shows continuing cost pressures in social care are largely driving the overall Council's forecast net overspend. This is a service that typically represents substantial Council spending and directly affects financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can control its largest discretionary spending line. Persistent adult social care overspends suggest systemic management weakness and represent a draw on the council's reserves and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £36.5m forecast net overspend; continuing pressure since prior year
findings.quote: Quarter 3 2025/26 budget monitoring identifies continuing cost pressures particularly within social care which are largely driving a forecast net overspend of £36.5m.

findings.headline: General reserves being drawn down to cover 2025-26 revenue overspend
findings.detail: General reserves are forecast at £48m as at 31 March 2026, but this is after an assumed drawdown to cover a 2025-26 revenue overspend identified in Quarter 3 monitoring. This means the overspend is eroding financial buffers.
findings.matters: Reserves provide essential liquidity and contingency for unexpected pressures; drawing them down to cover in-year revenue overspends reduces financial flexibility and resilience.
findings.figures: £48m general reserves balance (after drawdown)
findings.quote: £48m in general reserves, which is the estimated balance as at 31.03.26 after an assumed drawdown to fund a 2025-26 overspend

findings.headline: Council acknowledges maintenance and modernisation budget is insufficient for its estate
findings.detail: The new Asset Management Strategy recognises that the current Modernisation of Assets budget is insufficient for the scale of the Council's property portfolio. The strategy requires mandatory capital contributions to reserves specifically to cover long-term maintenance, indicating a known backlog.
findings.matters: Acknowledging insufficient maintenance budgets signals deferred maintenance liabilities and future capital spending pressures that may force additional borrowing or asset disposals.
findings.figures: Not specified; applies to all council estate assets
findings.quote: the current Modernisation of Assets budget is insufficient for the scale of KCC's estate

findings.headline: Council diverting £9m of capital receipts to balance revenue budget for 2026-27
findings.detail: The Council plans to use up to £9m from asset sales proceeds to plug the revenue budget shortfall, rather than invest in capital projects. This represents a diversion of capital resources to cover current spending pressures and effectively reduces capital funding available.
findings.matters: Using capital receipts to fund revenue is a sign of revenue budget strain and reduces the pool available for capital investment, requiring greater borrowing to maintain the capital programme.
findings.figures: £9m of capital receipts redirected from capital to revenue
findings.quote: The Council plans to use up to £9m of capital receipts (under the Government direction that allows revenue costs of projects that will reduce costs, increase revenue or support a more efficient provision of services to be funded from asset sale proceeds) to balance the 2026-27 revenue budget.

findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset sales have collapsed to near-zero, signalling end of disposal programme
findings.detail: Table 5 shows planned application of asset sale receipts falling from £15.94m cumulatively to just £0.35m in 2026-27. The Council acknowledges this reflects exhaustion of surplus assets, stating future receipts will depend on selling underutilised rather than surplus assets.
findings.matters: Asset sales are a traditional source of capital funding without revenue impact; their disappearance forces reliance on borrowing and constrains future capital flexibility.
findings.figures: Capital receipts from asset sales: £15.94m (prior years) to £0.35m (2026-27); £0.48m (2027-28); £0.55m (2028-29)
findings.quote: future receipts will increasingly come from underutilised assets rather than surplus ones

findings.headline: Borrowing to fund capital programme more than doubles to £76.84m in 2026-27
findings.detail: Borrowing rises sharply from £34.91m forecast for 2025-26 to £76.84m budgeted for 2026-27, representing over 120% growth and accounting for 22% of the total £350.51m capital programme. This increase occurs despite the Council explicitly stating that "bids requiring KCC funding are not currently being encouraged to mitigate against the challenging global and national financial situation."
findings.matters: A sudden doubling of borrowing increases the council's debt servicing costs and revenue burden, and suggests capital needs are outpacing available non-borrowed funding despite attempts to restrict them.
findings.figures: Borrowing: £34.91m (2025-26 forecast) to £76.84m (2026-27 budget); Total capital expenditure £350.51m
findings.quote: Bids requiring KCC funding are not currently being encouraged to mitigate against the challenging global and national financial situation, other than invest/spend to save bids.

findings.headline: Council has withdrawn Net Zero commitments amid shift to 50% match-funding requirement, creating £30m risk
findings.detail: Kent has formally withdrawn its commitment to deliver Net Zero 2030 and 2050 targets and no longer recognises a Climate Change Emergency. This occurs as government funding for net zero initiatives has shifted from 0-20% match funding to requiring 50% match funding. There is a risk of government penalties for missing national targets or the council incurring substantial unbudgeted costs through match funding or alternative compliance measures.
findings.matters: This signals a fundamental policy shift and creates ambiguity about future compliance costs. Government penalties or the need to fund half of net zero projects would create unforeseen pressure on an already strained budget.
findings.figures: £30m estimated exposure; match funding increased from 0-20% to 50%
findings.quote: KCC has formally withdrawn its commitment to deliver Net Zero targets for 2030 and 2050 and no longer recognises a Climate Change Emergency.

findings.headline: Waste infrastructure aging with £50m estimated exposure for capital replacement requiring significant borrowing
findings.detail: Several of Kent's Household Waste Recycling Centres and Waste Transfer Stations are life-expired (35-40 years old) and require major repair, replacement, or reconfiguration. District Local Plan housing targets will increase waste volumes, creating capacity pressures. The council may need to fund replacement of existing facilities and construct new sites, requiring significant capital borrowing if developer contributions are not secured.
findings.matters: This represents unfunded capital need that will increase the council's borrowing costs and pressure revenue budgets. If funding is not secured, waste will be processed at higher-cost disposal sites, perpetuating revenue pressure.
findings.figures: £50m estimated annual exposure; HWRC/WTS assets 35-40 years old
findings.quote: Several of KCC's Household Waste Recycling Centres (HWRCs) and Waste Transfer Stations (WTSs) are life-expired (35–40 years old) and require major repair, replacement, or reconfiguration.

findings.headline: £57.6m estimated exposure from failure to deliver agreed savings and income targets
findings.detail: The council is at risk of delays or failure in delivering planned savings and income targets due to operational challenges and external factors. This would create overspends requiring either compensating in-year savings or draws from reserves, creating recurring budget pressures in future years. The register identifies this as a "Likely" event (likelihood rating 4 out of 5).
findings.matters: Inability to deliver planned savings is a structural problem. If the council cannot execute its own financial plan, it signals weak operational control and an underlying deficit that cannot be closed, making recovery impossible without external intervention.
findings.figures: £57.6m estimated annual exposure
findings.quote: Delays or failure in delivering agreed savings and income targets due to changes in circumstances, operational challenges, or external factors.

findings.headline: General reserves forecast to fall below the council's own 5% minimum threshold
findings.detail: Current forecasts indicate general reserves could fall below the council's preferred minimum of 5%, driven by repeated overspends, rising demand-led costs, and reliance on one-off measures to balance budgets. The cumulative impact of prior-year overspends, in-year overspends, and savings slippage has created a reserves depletion spiral that will leave the council with minimal capacity to absorb financial shocks.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is a leading indicator of financial distress. Once reserves fall below minimum levels, the council loses the buffer to manage unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls, increasing the risk of emergency intervention or service collapse.
findings.figures: Preferred minimum 5%; forecast to fall below this level
findings.quote: Current forecasts indicate that general reserves could fall below the Council's preferred minimum of 5%.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care persistent overspends of £45-50m annually with structural sustainability risks
findings.detail: ASCH is identified as the single largest financial risk to the council, with overspends of £45m in 2024-25 and £49.7m forecast for 2025-26 (Q3). The council has adopted a new strategy to limit provider price uplifts to 0-3.6% and resist demand growth, but this introduces risks around provider sustainability and service capacity. If these pressures persist, the council will face severe constraints on setting a balanced budget and may need to cut other services.
findings.matters: These are recurring annual overspends of structural significance. The strategy to constrain costs may trigger provider exits from the market, reduce service quality, and leave the council unable to meet statutory duties—exposing it to legal challenge and reputational damage.
findings.figures: £45m overspend 2024-25; £49.7m forecast 2025-26; £68m annual exposure estimated
findings.quote: ASCH remains the single largest financial risk to the Council, with historic overspends exceeding £45m in 2024–25 and £49.7m forecast for 2025–26 (Q3 forecast).

findings.headline: DSG accumulated deficit forecast at £135m with no clear path to elimination by end of Safety Valve agreement
findings.detail: The council's Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block accumulated deficit is forecast to reach approximately £135m by end of 2025-26, with an in-year deficit of over £65m. The council is no longer on target to eliminate this deficit by the end of the current Safety Valve Agreement in 2027-28. The government's commitment to prevent local authority top-ups from 2028-29 onwards is contingent on councils demonstrating they can move to a financially sustainable position, which Kent is currently failing to do.
findings.matters: This is one of the two largest financial risks on the register and directly threatens the council's ability to set a balanced budget. If the Safety Valve agreement ends without clearing the deficit, the £135m+ could need to be reflected in the council's accounts in 2028-29, making it impossible to balance the budget.
findings.figures: £135m accumulated deficit forecast by end of 2025-26; £65m+ in-year deficit; Safety Valve agreement ends 2027-28
findings.quote: The DSG accumulated deficit at the end of 2025-26 is forecast to be around £135m with an in-year deficit of over £65m.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan shows unbalanced spending vs funding; may require Exceptional Financial Support from government
findings.detail: The indicative financial plans for 2027/28 and 2028/29 are not balanced within central government funding. The statement indicates that balancing from reserves would leave the council with inadequate reserves, and notes 'the Authority may need to seek Exceptional Financial Support from central Government' if solutions are not identified.
findings.matters: If a council of this size requires exceptional government financial support, it signals systemic financial stress beyond normal management; this is a material structural concern for a lender assessing medium-term sustainability.
findings.figures: No specific medium-term funding gap quantified in this document; described as 'significant additional financial challenge'; 2027/28 and 2028/29 not balanced within settlement
findings.quote: The indicative future spending plans are not balanced within the additional funding from central Government in the multi-year settlement. Balancing the medium-term shortfalls from reserves would in all likelihood leave the Council with inadequate reserves. If these solutions are not identified and agreed as part of developing 2027/28 budget the Authority may need to seek Exceptional Financial Support from central Government.
